name: Lateral Epicondylalgia (Tennis Elbow)
summary: Load-related lateral elbow pain involving the common wrist-extensor tendon, especially extensor carpi radialis brevis.

looksLike: Pain pouring kettle or shaking hands
redFlags: Joint locking or severe ROM loss
firstSteps: Begin pain-monitored isometric or isotonic wrist extensor loading

assess: Tenderness at lateral epicondyle/common extensor tendon
Pain with resisted wrist extension or middle-finger extension
Reduced grip strength due to pain
Pain with gripping and resisted wrist extension
Cervical/radial nerve screen when symptoms are atypical

tests.name: Mill Test
tests.purpose: Passively lengthen common wrist extensor tendon.

stages.label: Load Calibration
stages.goal: Reduce repeated aggravating load while maintaining tendon activity.
do: Begin pain-monitored isometric or isotonic wrist extensor loading

stages.label: Progressive Tendon & Grip Strength
stages.goal: Build wrist extensor, supinator and grip capacity.

stages.label: Task-Specific Return
moveOn: Full target task volume tolerated without prolonged flare

logic: Progressive wrist-extensor and grip loading is central.
Use pain-free grip change to judge whether an adjunct such as MWM is useful.
Screen cervical/radial nerve contribution when the pattern is atypical.
mechanism: Sudden increase in manual or racquet load
investigations: Imaging considered for atypical, traumatic or persistent cases where another diagnosis is suspected.
manual: Elbow/forearm mobilization with movement may reduce pain short term in selected patients.
Lateral elbow MWM when it improves pain-free grip
Soft-tissue techniques to extensor mass as adjunct
Lateral elbow MWM can be used if it immediately improves pain-free grip.
Soft-tissue/friction techniques are optional adjuncts and should remain tolerable.
Do not aggressively friction an irritable tendon.
modalities: Avoid making ultrasound/electrotherapy the main treatment.
Counterforce strap may help some patients temporarily during activity.
Counterforce strap may be trialed for activity
Electrotherapy is optional rather than primary
Counterforce strap may be trialed during provoking tasks.
dosing: Gripping: 2–3 sets × 8–15 submaximal reps, progressing load.
progression: Increase load as pain-free grip improves.
Progress speed, tool/racquet demand and endurance later.
Use next-day tendon response to adjust dose.
mistakes: Missing radial tunnel or cervical source
pearls: Resisted wrist extension + lateral epicondyle pain = classic pattern.
Treat capacity and load tolerance, not tenderness alone.
education: Explain tendon load tolerance and gradual strengthening.
Temporarily modify the heaviest gripping, then reintroduce it.
escalation: Medical review for persistent atypical pain, neurological findings or failure after a well-adhered program

tests.name: Cozen Test
tests.patientPosition: Sitting with elbow supported and forearm pronated or neutral.
tests.handPlacement: Stabilize elbow; resist wrist extension/radial deviation over dorsum of hand.
procedure: Ask patient to make a fist.
Patient extends/radially deviates wrist against resistance.

tests.name: Mill Test
tests.purpose: Passively lengthen common wrist extensor tendon.
procedure: Extend elbow while maintaining the stretch.

tests.name: Maudsley Test
tests.handPlacement: Apply resistance to middle finger extension.
procedure: Ask patient to extend middle finger against resistance.
tests.interpretation: Supports lateral epicondylalgia but radial tunnel differential should be considered.

story.headline: The coffee mug that became an elbow strength test
story.scene: A carpenter lifts his morning tea and winces at the outside of his elbow. He's convinced it must be 'tennis elbow,' although his only racket lives in a cupboard.
story.dialogue: Patient: 'I haven't played tennis in ten years!' Therapist: 'Good news: the elbow didn't check your sports membership.'
story.clue: Local lateral elbow pain aggravated by gripping or resisted wrist extension fits lateral epicondylalgia, often linked to wrist-extensor tendon loading.
story.twist: Pain over the elbow can also come from cervical or radial nerve sources; neurologic signs and atypical findings change the examination.
story.aha: A painful grip tells you about load tolerance, not whether the patient owns a tennis racket.
story.patientTranslation: The tendon near the outside of your elbow may be sensitive to gripping and lifting. We usually work on comfortable movement, gradually stronger gripping and changes to heavy repetitive tasks.
story.clinicianReasoning: Assess resisted wrist extension, gripping capacity, cervical/radial nerve screening and functional irritability. Prescribe progressive tendon loading with practical task modification; avoid promising a passive 'quick fix.'
story.rehabBridge: Adjust painful gripping loads → build wrist-extensor and forearm capacity → restore work and sport-specific lifting endurance.
story.question: For typical lateral epicondylalgia without red flags, what is a sensible core strategy?
options: Only passive modalities with no strengthening
Graded forearm loading plus task-specific education
story.explanation: Progressive loading and education address tendon-related function; passive modalities alone do not replace rebuilding capacity.
